reading.body:
Jimmy Panetta's AI record is mostly money and cosponsorships, not floor leadership: 18 dated events, of which 10 are political committee contributions and 5 are votes or cosponsorships on AI-related measures.

The contributions come from the same small set of companies repeatedly. Google's committee appears four times, Amazon's three, Oracle once, and Intel once as a negative entry of $-1,500. The amounts are small, between $90 and $3,000, which is the scale of routine committee giving rather than a signal of any single transaction. The bills are more varied: workforce readiness, facial recognition, antisemitic content on AI platforms, and a data center tax measure. That last one is the only item in the record that touches the physical layer of AI, the buildings and power that data centers require, and it appears once, as a cosponsorship.

For AI specifically, the pattern matters because compute buildout is now decided in exactly this kind of legislation. A member who cosponsors a data center tax bill and takes money from the companies that build and supply data centers is participating in the same policy area from two directions. The record does not show that one caused the other, and the page says so directly. It also does not show committee assignments, floor speeches, or any position on permitting, transmission, or power supply, which are the constraints that determine whether data centers get built at all.

What the data cannot support is any conclusion about influence or intent. Ten contributions over roughly eighteen months, all small and all from a handful of firms, is a normal pattern for a member on a relevant committee. The record is a chronology, not an argument.
